summary:
FireWatch Brasil turns two incompatible NASA satellite fire records into one consistent 23-year fire history for Brazil, and puts it in a web platform anyone can explore.

MODIS (1 km pixels, since 2000) and VIIRS (375 m, since 2012) see fires very differently, so joining their records creates a fake jump in 2012. We processed 30.1 million NASA FIRMS hotspots: applied the same cleaning rules to every satellite, merged hotspots into fire events, matched MODIS and VIIRS detections, and trained a gradient-boosting model on 2012-2016, when both satellites flew together, to convert MODIS counts into VIIRS units. Tested on years it never saw, it is accurate to 3.4% nationally and 8.5% per state-month, with -0.2% bias, and every value comes with a 90% uncertainty band.

The result is one record from January 2003 to November 2026 for Brazil and all 27 states. Our web app shows it as a fire map, historical analytics, a burning calendar, research tools, and live NASA FIRMS monitoring that compares today's fires with the normal for that date. Researchers, journalists and decision-makers can finally answer, fairly, "is Brazil burning more than before?"
details:
What it does:

FireWatch Brasil builds one consistent fire record for every place in Brazil from January 2003 to November 2026, in a single unit (VIIRS S-NPP fire events), and makes it explorable through a web platform. It solves the core problem of the challenge: MODIS and VIIRS detect fires differently (1 km vs 375 m pixels), so their raw records cannot be compared. Simply joining them creates an artificial jump in 2012 when VIIRS started.

How it works:

1. Load: 30.1 million NASA FIRMS hotspots (MODIS Collection 6.1 2003-2026, VIIRS S-NPP 2012-Oct 2026, NOAA-20 for Nov 2026).

2. Clean: the same confidence rules for every satellite; factories, gas flares and offshore platforms (persistent static heat sources) are removed.

3. Fire events: hotspots within 1 km of each other on the same day are merged into one fire event (graph clustering with a k-d tree). This removes the pixel-size difference between sensors.

4. Matching: MODIS and VIIRS fire events within 2 km are labelled MATCHED, MODIS-only or VIIRS-only.

5. Grid: 0.25-degree squares (about 28 km) by month, 11,209 squares x 287 months, each assigned to its Brazilian state.

6. Model: a gradient-boosting regressor (scikit-learn HistGradientBoosting, Poisson loss for counts) learns how many fire events VIIRS sees given what MODIS saw in a square and its neighbours, fire intensity (FRP), month and location. It was trained on 2012-2016, when both satellites flew together.

7. Validation: leave-one-year-out testing, where the model never sees the year it is scored on. We compared five approaches (fixed ratio, seasonal ratio, regional-seasonal ratio, Poisson GLM, gradient boosting). Gradient boosting won with 8.5% error per state-month, 3.4% per national month, -0.2% bias and R2 0.997. Each value has an empirical 90% uncertainty band.

8. Build the record: MODIS converted by the model before 2012, real VIIRS S-NPP after, 53 satellite outage days gap-filled, and NOAA-20 scaled by 0.951 (a factor we measured) after S-NPP ended.

The web platform:

- Fire Map: harmonized fire density for any period 2003-2026, fire events coloured by which satellite saw them, raw hotspots, a 3D globe, and filters by date, state or a drawn area.

- Historical Analytics: year-by-year comparison, each month against its 5-year median, anomaly %, and a state ranking.

- Fire Calendar: every month since 2003, coloured by fire density or by deviation from normal.

- Research tools: daily anomaly calendar, climatology envelope, MODIS-VIIRS matching map, raw vs harmonized record, and CSV/JSON exports.

- Live monitoring: the backend pulls the NASA FIRMS API every 15 minutes, runs the same pipeline, and rates every state against its normal for that date (for example, "Acre 2.19x normal, ELEVATED").

Benefits and intended impact:

- For the first time, any year, state or month in Brazil can be compared fairly from 2003 to today without sensor artefacts.

- Live fire counts gain context: not just "1,653 fires" but "0.78x normal for mid-November".

- Researchers, journalists, environmental agencies and policymakers can study long-term trends, check whether a fire season is unusual, and download the data for their own analysis.

- The method can be reused for other countries and future satellites (for example NOAA-21).

Tools and languages:

- Python: pandas, NumPy, SciPy (k-d tree, connected components), scikit-learn (gradient boosting), PyArrow (Parquet), Matplotlib, Jupyter.

- Backend: FastAPI and Uvicorn (REST API for the record, analytics, exports and live data).

- Frontend: React and Vite, MapLibre GL JS (3D globe), Leaflet and leaflet.heat, Chart.js.

- Data: NASA FIRMS archive and NRT API, IBGE-derived Brazilian state boundaries; map tiles from OpenStreetMap, CARTO and Esri.

- No special hardware: everything runs on a normal laptop.

What makes it creative:

- We harmonize at the level of fire events, not raw pixels, so the sensors are compared on equal terms before any model is applied.

- The model learns a relationship that changes with place, season and neighbouring fires, instead of using one fixed ratio.

- We turned a data-science result into a usable product: a burning calendar, anomaly ratings and live monitoring built on the same harmonized baseline.

Factors we considered:

- Honesty about uncertainty: every converted value has a 90% band, and we report errors from data the model never saw.

- Sensor drift: training on later years added a -2% to -3% bias because the ageing MODIS satellites drift, so we kept the cleanest overlap years (2012-2016).

- Limitations: it counts fire events, not burned area; fire intensity (FRP) is not harmonized; single 28 km squares are noisy, while states and regions are reliable (3-8% error).

- Responsible use: satellite fire detections include agricultural burning, so the platform is not an emergency alert service and says so.

- Usability: the same methods are documented in a notebook, an API and a methods report, so others can reproduce and extend the work.

Future plans:

- Live data that builds the record automatically: today, our backend already pulls NASA FIRMS near-real-time data every 15 minutes and harmonizes it on the fly (same cleaning, fire-event clustering, MODIS-VIIRS matching and NOAA-20 conversion as our record), but it only keeps it in memory for the live panel. Next, we will store every harmonized update permanently in a PostgreSQL database with the PostGIS extension for spatial queries.

- One growing record: each new day of harmonized fire events will be appended to the same tables as our 2003-2026 record (daily per state, monthly per 0.25° square), so the dataset keeps extending itself instead of being rebuilt by hand. When NASA later publishes the final archive version of those days, we will re-process them and replace the near-real-time values.

- The platform on top of the database: the Fire Map, Analytics, Fire Calendar and Research tools will read directly from PostgreSQL, so every page always shows the record up to today, and anomaly ratings use the full, continuously updated history.

- More satellites and regions: add NOAA-21 as it matures, extend coverage to all of South America, and add burned-area products alongside fire counts.

- Open access: a public API and scheduled exports so researchers and agencies can download the always-current harmonized record.
